And the receipt still says exact-noiseless construction, so this is a production-parameter-size execution receipt, not a noisy bootstrap-key robustness proof or a blanket security audit.
scenes.headline: Production parameter size. Two rows.
scenes.subhead: Initial run · N=1024 · PASS · 2.7189 seconds

scenes.voiceover: One more receipt belongs beside the authored panels: the literal terminal rerun filmed after the script was drafted. This is a real Bash pseudo-terminal at normal speed. It types the complete Verilog, verifies a byte-for-byte match with the tracked source, synthesizes three lookup tables, checks both endpoints, exhausts all thirty-two clear rows, exhausts all thirty-two encrypted rows at N sixteen, and runs two deterministic rows at N one thousand twenty-four on Metal. The values differ slightly from the first receipt. The initial run recorded zero point zero zero eight nine seconds and two point seven one eight nine seconds. This filmed rerun recorded zero point zero zero nine five seconds and two point five three two zero seconds. Both runs passed. They are two observations, not a timing distribution or evidence of stable performance. The footage proves that these commands executed; the static panels remain the readable scientific receipts.
scenes.label: Filmed rerun · 2026-09-04 · normal speed

scenes.voiceover: Put the layers beside one another and the result is useful without being inflated. Yosys mapped a five-input majority function into three lookup tables. The clear path matched all thirty-two inputs. The encrypted demonstration path matched all thirty-two again. The production-parameter-size Metal path matched two endpoint rows. The later filmed rerun repeated those outcomes, with separate timing observations. Outside those receipts are the stronger claims: no multiparty voting protocol, no proof that the host learns nothing from timing or metadata, no noisy-key result, and no exhaustive sweep at one thousand twenty-four. The circuit works in the harness. The surrounding election system has not been built, and the episode will not pretend otherwise.
scenes.headline: What the receipts prove
bullets: Yosys: 5 inputs → 3 mapped tables → 1 output
Clear path: 32 of 32 patterns match in both runs
Encrypted N=16 path: 32 of 32 match in both runs
Metal N=1024 path: 2 of 2 endpoints match in both runs

scenes.voiceover: One more thing, because scale is the honest test of a compiler. Everything so far used three lookup tables. The same path also takes a real processor: a RISC-V core synthesized to four thousand seven hundred eighty-five lookup tables and one thousand five hundred sixty-five flip-flops. That matters because flip-flops mean state. The circuit has to be clocked, and every encrypted register has to survive every tick. The program is deliberately tiny: put one in a register, store it to memory, read it back. If encrypted state were broken, that sequence would fail immediately. Here is the boundary, though. The host implements the memory, so it sees instruction addresses and data. Only the processor itself is evaluated encrypted.
scenes.headline: Three lookup tables, then a processor
scenes.subhead: 4785 lookup tables · 1565 flip-flops · encrypted state
scenes.kicker: Coda · the same path, much bigger

scenes.voiceover: Same compiler, same encrypted evaluator, a very different circuit. The capture compiles both designs live: the majority circuit is five inputs, three lookup tables, no state. The processor is a hundred and two inputs, four thousand seven hundred eighty-five lookup tables, and one thousand five hundred sixty-five flip-flops. Then it runs that tiny program under encryption for forty-eight ticks. Watch the program counter advance by four each fetch. At tick sixteen the store writes one to address zero. At tick twenty-five the host serves that same one back. Forty-eight of forty-eight ticks matched the clear model, including every flip-flop, in two point four eight two eight seconds. And the honest part: this ran on CPU, at four modeled bits, and the host is the memory.
scenes.label: Coda · encrypted RISC-V · normal speed

scenes.voiceover: The worthwhile part is not that majority is a difficult function. It is that the privacy boundary is understandable, the input space is small enough to exhaust, and the production-size claim can be separated cleanly from the demonstration. The source, generated netlist, six full logs, curated receipt, two literal captures with their own manifests and transcripts, commands, dates, and hashes are all preserved. On a matching toolchain, there is a path back from the sentence to the run. Five encrypted bits entered this harness. One decision bit was revealed. A three-table vote and a whole processor came out of the same compiler. Everything stronger remains outside the receipt. That is how a small experiment earns an episode.
scenes.headline: The path back is the point
scenes.subhead: Source. Netlist. Six logs. One bounded result.

episodes.title: One Callsign, Three Acts
episodes.youtubeTitle: GNU Radio Recovered a Demo Callsign — Then a Yosys Circuit Matched It
episodes.description: A literal, reproducible closed-loop experiment sends CQ CQ CQ DE AB0CDE AB0CDE K through locally generated BPSK-like IQ and a simulated GNU Radio channel at noise_voltage=0.0. All 27 bytes return exactly; a fixed six-byte, 48-input, 47-LUT Yosys circuit reports callsign completions at payload bytes 17 and 24. A clear scalar host loop then produces 908 expected and observed hits across 10,000 evaluations of 22 unique windows. Finally, one AB0CDE window runs on the N=8 encrypted demonstration path, with engine and key setup excluded from its timer. No antenna, OTA signal, interception, general regex engine, native tensor batch, encrypted stream, or production-security claim is involved. The literal terminal capture, full raw log, hashes, and reproduction commands are preserved. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: This episode begins with a demonstration callsign and ends with a receipt. I built a circuit that recognizes exactly six ASCII bytes: A B zero C D E. Then I gave the same circuit three deliberately different jobs. First, match callsigns recovered from a local GNU Radio loop through the clear Boolean oracle. Second, repeat recovered windows through that same clear path. Third, freeze one callsign and evaluate that one window on the encrypted demonstration path. Those are three acts, not one blended claim. The signal is local, the footage is literal, and every boundary stays on screen.
scenes.headline: One callsign. Three acts.
scenes.subhead: Local IQ. Recovered bytes. A circuit says yes.

scenes.voiceover: Here is the channel before any circuit sees a byte. GNU Radio starts from a finite vector in memory. It maps bits to plus or minus one, repeats each symbol four times, creates complex baseband samples, passes them through the channel-model block, hard-slices the result, and finds an A A fifty-five preamble to recover byte alignment. The transmitted payload is C Q, C Q, C Q, D E, A B zero C D E, A B zero C D E, K. For the filmed receipt, noise voltage is zero point zero. Twenty-seven bytes went in and the same twenty-seven came back, with zero byte differences. This is a deterministic local loop. There was no antenna, no over-the-air signal, and nothing was intercepted.
scenes.headline: A radio chain with no radio link
scenes.subhead: CQ CQ CQ DE AB0CDE AB0CDE K · 27 bytes out, 27 bytes back

scenes.voiceover: The detector is intentionally concrete. Six eight-bit ports are compared with the ASCII values for A, B, zero, C, D, and E. That makes forty-eight input bits and one match output. Yosys and ABC lower the authored Verilog into forty-seven two-input lookup-table cells, and the Yosys check pass reports zero problems. HELUT does not receive a string search function. It receives that generated lookup-table graph. The rolling helper learns its six-byte window from ports named char zero through char five, packs each byte least-significant bit first, and ticks the netlist. This is an exact, case-sensitive, fixed-literal circuit. Calling it a general regular-expression engine would claim something we did not build.
scenes.headline: Six bytes become forty-eight wires
scenes.subhead: Exact ASCII literal · 47 two-input lookup tables · one match bit

scenes.voiceover: After GNU Radio stops, Python feeds the recovered payload to HELUT one byte at a time. The first five bytes only warm the six-byte window. A match appears when the final E arrives. In this payload, the first callsign occupies zero-based byte positions twelve through seventeen. The second occupies nineteen through twenty-four. So the expected completion positions are seventeen and twenty-four. The clear netlist oracle reports exactly that list. The runner also scans the recovered bytes in software and compares against the callsign positions in the transmitted payload. Both comparisons must agree or the command exits with failure. In the filmed run, the recovered bytes were exact and both callsign windows survived.
scenes.headline: Both callsigns land exactly
scenes.subhead: Match completion indices: [17, 24]
scenes.kicker: Act I · recovered stream · clear oracle

scenes.voiceover: Act two asks a different question: can the host-to-library hinge repeat the clear circuit many times and keep the answer straight? A twenty-seven-byte payload contains twenty-two overlapping six-byte windows. The runner cycles those windows in order until it has made ten thousand scalar calls. Ten thousand is four hundred fifty-four complete cycles of twenty-two, plus twelve extra windows. Each complete cycle contains the two callsigns, and those first twelve remainder windows contain neither. Four hundred fifty-four times two gives nine hundred eight expected hits. HELUT reports nine hundred eight. The filmed wall observation is one hundred thirteen point three four milliseconds. But this is not batch acceleration. It is a clear scalar host loop, not a native tensor batch and not encrypted throughput.
scenes.headline: Ten thousand calls, one at a time
scenes.subhead: 22 unique windows · 908 expected · 908 observed

scenes.voiceover: Only act three enters the encrypted demonstration mode. The runner selects the first recovered A B zero C D E window, opens the fixed-seed N eight engine, and then starts the stopwatch around the six feed calls. Five calls warm the window; the sixth evaluates the circuit. The decrypted demonstration result is one, matching the expected bit. The filmed evaluation observation is one point one milliseconds, but engine and key setup happened before that timer. N eight is a tiny demonstration parameter, not production security. One frozen window is not an encrypted radio stream. The honest result is narrower and still useful: this generated forty-seven-table circuit returns the right bit on one encrypted demonstration input.
scenes.headline: Encrypt one callsign, not the stream
scenes.subhead: AB0CDE · N=8 demonstration · result 1

scenes.voiceover: This is the literal run, not a reconstruction. First, the authored Verilog and its hash. Next, Yosys reloads the generated netlist: forty-eight input bits, forty-seven lookup tables, one output, and zero check problems. Then GNU Radio creates the local I Q stream and recovers all twenty-seven bytes. HELUT reports the callsign at completion positions seventeen and twenty-four. The final screen separates the other acts: ten thousand clear scalar windows, nine hundred eight expected and observed hits; then one A B zero C D E window on the N eight encrypted demonstration path. The tape ends with the no-antenna verdict and hashes of the source, netlist, runner, and full raw log.
scenes.label: Literal run · 2026-09-04 · normal speed

scenes.voiceover: The durable receipt now fits in four rows. Radio first: twenty-seven transmitted bytes, twenty-seven recovered bytes, zero differences, and callsign completions at seventeen and twenty-four. Circuit next: six exact bytes become forty-eight input bits, forty-seven two-input lookup tables, and one result bit. Repetition next: ten thousand clear scalar window evaluations, built from twenty-two unique windows, produce nine hundred eight expected and observed hits. Encryption last: one recovered A B zero C D E window enters the N eight demonstration path and returns one. The tape, M P four, authored source, canonical netlist, runner, transcript, manifest, and complete unfiltered log all have hashes. The raw log is preserved beside the capture rather than existing only under an ignored build directory.

bullets: 27 / 27 bytes exact · callsign completions [17, 24]
6 bytes · 48 input bits · 47 LUT2 cells · 1 output
10,000 clear scalar windows · 22 unique · 908 / 908

scenes.voiceover: Now draw the box around the result. The source was a local vector and no antenna was used, so this is not reception or interception. The channel-model block was present, but noise voltage was zero for deterministic footage, so the run does not establish tolerance to noise. The circuit recognizes one fixed literal, so it is not a general regex engine. Acts one and two use the clear Boolean oracle. Ten thousand means scalar calls over twenty-two repeating source windows, not a native tensor batch and not encrypted throughput. Act three encrypts one window at N eight; it is not an encrypted stream, and N eight is not a production security parameter. Finally, every timing number is one local observation. The receipts prove execution and agreement, not a performance distribution.
scenes.headline: What this run is not

Not a channel-noise tolerance result

scenes.voiceover: That separation is the point. GNU Radio recovered a recognizable payload through a local baseband loop. A generated lookup-table circuit found both copies of the callsign on the clear path. The same clear circuit survived ten thousand scalar invocations with the exact expected count. Then one recovered window crossed the encrypted demonstration path and returned the right bit. None of those facts needs an antenna story, a batch-performance story, or a production-security story to be interesting. The source, netlist, literal footage, full output, commands, and hashes are preserved. A B zero C D E went through the machine, and the path back to every sentence is still there.
scenes.headline: One fixed circuit, bounded three ways
scenes.subhead: Signal recovered. Callsign matched. Claims kept separate.

episodes.title: The Skeptic's Benchmark
episodes.youtubeTitle: Does Tensorized Verilog Actually Help? An Honest HELUT Benchmark
episodes.description: A technically informed skeptic asks the right questions: what problem does tensorizing a synthesized circuit solve, is it more efficient than native HDL execution, and why target Apple silicon? This episode answers with the current receipt, the current gaps, and the architectural case for unified memory. A 688-LUT, 26-DFF Enigma M3 netlist runs through HELUT's trivial, noise-free N=1024 Metal path and agrees exactly with the clear oracle on a 25-letter transcript, in three of three runs. The saved log separates compile, first-tick JIT, steady ticks, stream time, and resident memory, and it reports a median with its spread rather than one number. Apple silicon matters here because host orchestration, Metal shaders, and MPSGraph allocate through shared buffers in one physical memory pool, which suits iterative Enigma candidate, scoring, and survivor workflows without claiming that synchronization is free. The episode does not claim encryption, distinct-lane batch throughput, superiority over Verilator, CXXRTL, or a discrete GPU, or a cross-platform result. It pre-registers the comparisons required to answer those questions honestly. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: A skeptic on Reddit asked the three questions this project has to answer. Hardware simulators already reproduce Verilog and V H D L accurately, so why turn a circuit into tensors? Is that actually faster than compiling H D L to native code? And if it is not, why should anyone care which chip it runs on? I will take those in order, starting from the assumption that native execution wins. What follows is one measured receipt, one caveat that undercuts the most quotable number in the repository, and a written-down experiment that could kill the performance thesis outright.
scenes.headline: Does tensorized Verilog actually help?
scenes.subhead: Start with the null hypothesis: native wins.

scenes.voiceover: First, remove a category error. HELUT is not a replacement for an event-driven H D L simulator. Yosys does the front-end and synthesis work, and A B C, the logic mapper Yosys calls, packs the resulting gates into lookup tables. HELUT picks up after that, from a two-state netlist of lookup tables, flip-flops, and ports. It has no model of behavioral Verilog, propagation delay, signal strength, or the four-state X and Z values a real simulator tracks. Bit accuracy, then, is not the selling point. Verilator and Icarus already own that job. The open question is what a restricted Boolean graph gains by being tensors: batching independent instances, reuse on a Metal graph substrate, sharing one representation with the encrypted path, or turning truth tables into a continuous search space.
scenes.headline: HELUT does not simulate arbitrary Verilog
scenes.subhead: Yosys first · two-state LUT and DFF netlist second
scenes.kicker: Define the object before timing it

scenes.voiceover: The tensor representation adds two independent axes. B is how many copies of the circuit ride along together. N is how many coefficients stand in for a single logical wire. N equals one is the smallest Boolean shape there is. N equals one thousand twenty-four matches the polynomial size the encrypted side of this project uses, though a constant-filled, noise-free vector at that size is still not encrypted data. Those axes give experiments a graph-shaped substrate that scalar simulation was never designed around. What they do not give is a speedup. A tensor can expose parallel work. Whether the machine then executes that work efficiently is a measurement, not a definition.
scenes.headline: Batch instances and wire degree
scenes.subhead: B copies of a circuit · N coefficients per encoded wire

scenes.voiceover: Here is what the repository can defend today. The synthesized Enigma M three graph holds six hundred eighty-eight lookup tables, twenty-six flip-flops, ten inputs, and eight outputs. I ran the N one thousand twenty-four, B one configuration three times on an M four Max. Median compile: zero point zero three eight three seconds. The first tick cost zero point three zero seven four seconds, because that tick pays to build and specialize the Metal kernels, the just-in-time cost. The nine ticks after it averaged zero point zero one four eight seconds, which the harness prints as sixty-seven point four nine ticks per second. Then a clear oracle, an independent scalar simulator in Swift that reads the same netlist and never touches the G P U, and the Metal path both produced K E I N E B E S O N D E R E N E R E I G N I S S E. All twenty-five letters matched, in all three runs. Why a median instead of a single number? Because the same netlist and tensor shape logged sixty-six to seventy-two ticks per second in archived August runs, and three cold passes earlier today logged about fifty-one. One number here would be fiction.
scenes.label: ARCHIVED RECEIPT PLAYBACK · preserved 2026-09-05 log · not a fresh timing run

scenes.voiceover: Now the caveat that undercuts the most quotable number in the repository. The clock benchmark fills every batch lane with the same encoded value. Enable is held at one, reset follows a scripted schedule, and every other primary input sits at zero. Output tensors do get written, but the timed loop never reads them back and never hashes them per lane. So the existing B scaling table measures graph shape, allocation, synchronization, and memory pressure. It does not measure useful throughput over one thousand distinct vectors, and describing it as a thousand-way verified simulation would be a lie. Three things have to change before a batching claim is allowed: every lane doing independent work, a canonical checksum over ordered outputs and final state, and a deliberately corrupted bit that makes the checksum fail.
scenes.headline: The existing batch sweep repeats one feed
scenes.subhead: B=1000 is not yet 1000 independently checked vectors
scenes.kicker: The number that cannot be oversold

scenes.voiceover: There is no Verilator benchmark in this repository, and none for C X X R T L, the C plus plus simulation backend Yosys ships, either. Not over the same synthesized artifact, not over the same stimulus. The clear Swift simulator is an oracle: a per-bit interpreter walking dictionaries. It is deliberately simple so it can be trusted, which also makes it useless as a performance baseline. Every timing table in the repo compares HELUT against other HELUT configurations. So the literal answer to the question is that HELUT has not established that tensor execution beats H D L compiled to native code. That gap is testable, which is the only reason it is worth admitting out loud. A credible series shows native winning where native wins, prices the setup and the memory, and saves the word crossover for a point where the same checked work actually changes the ordering.
scenes.headline: Is it faster than native HDL?
scenes.subhead: Current answer: the repository has not established that

scenes.voiceover: The missing comparison has a contract, and writing it down before measuring is the whole point. Three circuits: a tiny combinational control, a medium lookup-table workload, and a sequential design with independent state per lane. Two native baselines: one built from authored R T L, one built from the same post-A B C graph HELUT consumes, so nobody can blame the mapper for the result. One corpus, deterministic and lane-distinct, fed to every backend. Outputs consumed inside the timed region, then hashed outside it, over ordered outputs and final state. Flip one expected bit and the checksum gate has to fail, or the gate is decoration. Then sweep batch size with total useful work held constant, and report all of it: build time, graph compile, first tick, steady compute, end-to-end break-even, vectors per second, peak resident memory, the spread across repeated trials, and every crash or out-of-memory point.
scenes.headline: Same circuit. Same work. Same digest.
scenes.subhead: Verilator · post-ABC native · HELUT · repeated trials

scenes.voiceover: Why Apple silicon? The practical answer is that it is the hardware I own, and a lot of other people own it too. The architectural answer is unified memory. HELUT's host code, its hand-written Metal compute shaders, and Metal Performance Shaders Graph all allocate through shared Metal buffers backed by one physical memory pool, instead of treating C P U memory and discrete V R A M as two separately staged worlds. The host writes inputs and state, a shader or a graph reads those same allocations, and the host inspects results after synchronization. The G P U also draws on the machine's whole memory capacity rather than a fixed V R A M budget. None of that makes movement or synchronization free, and none of it is a speedup. What it does is make tightly coupled, memory-hungry hybrid experiments practical on hardware you can buy in a shop.
scenes.headline: Unified memory is the big win
scenes.subhead: Host code · Metal shaders · MPSGraph · shared buffers
scenes.kicker: The architectural reason · one memory pool

scenes.voiceover: Enigma makes that pattern concrete. Host code organizes rotor, ring, and starting-position settings, plugboard pairs, and candidate populations. Wide Metal kernels sweep many settings or scoring lanes at once. The host then filters survivors, tightens constraints, breeds the next generation, and starts another round. With shared buffers those phases can live in one memory pool instead of paying a staging tax at every boundary. Large candidate tensors can spend real unified memory. But capacity is not throughput, and the repository has a receipt that proves it. At N one thousand twenty-four and B one thousand, resident memory peaked near six gigabytes and the tick rate fell to thirteen point six two per second, against roughly sixty-nine at B equals one. So the defensible claim is that unified memory opens this design space. Beating a discrete G P U inside it is a separate measurement nobody here has taken.
scenes.headline: Build candidates on the CPU; sweep them on the GPU
scenes.subhead: Settings · tables · ciphertext · scores · survivors · repeat
scenes.kicker: Why Enigma makes the architecture visible

scenes.voiceover: So what does HELUT actually solve today? It bridges supported Yosys lookup-table graphs into a Metal tensor substrate, and on the circuit I tested, that substrate agrees with an independent clear oracle. It also gives host-orchestrated, G P U-evaluated experiments a shared-buffer home on one commodity memory pool. Those two facts establish that the bridge works, and they explain why this target is interesting. Neither one establishes superiority over native simulation. The batch result is not yet lane-distinct throughput. The Apple result is an architectural argument, not a verdict on architectures. Every open row on this list has a specific experiment attached to it, which is the only reason I am comfortable leaving them open.
scenes.headline: The current verdict
bullets: Proved: supported Yosys LUT/DFF graphs execute on Metal
Proved: clear oracle and Metal outputs agree, 3 of 3 runs
Implemented: shared-buffer CPU/GPU workflows on unified memory
Open: native speedup, lane-distinct batch throughput
Not claimed: full HDL semantics or Apple exclusivity

scenes.voiceover: The tensor path gets more interesting when the circuit is not merely executed. A lookup table can be lifted out of zeros and ones into continuous values, searched against a target, and pushed back toward discrete hardware. That is melt and freeze, and it arrives with its own bill. Did the frozen circuit stay correct? Did the topology change? Did the resource count improve? Will Yosys take the emitted result back? And what happens when the search refuses to go binary? Episode fifteen puts the passing two-bit control, the round-trip checker, its negative control, and the failed M four run on the same screen.
scenes.headline: If not better simulation, then what?
scenes.subhead: Next: melt the truth tables, freeze them again, and inspect the proof.

episodes.title: Melt. Freeze. Prove.
episodes.youtubeTitle: Melt and Freeze a Hardware Circuit — What HELUT Actually Proves
episodes.description: HELUT's melt/freeze path is shown as implemented: fixed-topology LUT truth tables are lifted from binary entries to Float32 values, selected LUTs are searched with evolutionary mutation and crossover, and a final threshold may return the mutable region to discrete zero-or-one tables when target fitness is preserved. Rerun on 2026-09-05, the deterministic two-bit-adder control passes in 1.092 s inside a six-test freeze-mask suite with zero failures. A separate identity emit-to-Yosys round trip checks 48 output bits over all 16 input assignments, and a one-bit INIT corruption produces four detected mismatches. Those are separate receipts: the current tree emits searched elites but never re-synthesizes and re-proves them, does not mutate topology, and does not establish area or depth improvement over Yosys/ABC. An archived M4 targeted-melt failure remains visible. Epoch C69.

scenes.voiceover: Melt and freeze sounds dramatic, so let me take the drama out first. A lookup table in HELUT holds truth-table entries that are normally exact zeros and ones. Melting means letting selected entries become floating-point values in between, then searching those values against a target. Freezing means pushing them back to exact binary. Proving means checking the resulting discrete circuit independently, with a tool that had no part in the search. The repository demonstrates each of those links, and it is missing the join between two of them. This episode shows the controlled pass, the checker that catches corruption, the large experiment that failed, and the exact sentence where a general simplification claim would outrun the evidence.
scenes.headline: Melt. Freeze. Prove.
scenes.subhead: Continuous truth tables are useful only if the discrete circuit survives.

scenes.voiceover: What melts is the I N I T table inside a lookup-table block. I N I T is the Verilog parameter that spells out a table's truth values, and TensorLUT pads every supported table to sixty-four Float thirty-two entries, six inputs being the widest cell it accepts. Evaluation uses the multilinear extension: each of the sixty-four entries is weighted by how strongly the inputs point at its corner of the cube. Feed it exact zeros and ones and only one weight is nonzero, so it returns the same entry Boolean logic would. Feed it fractions and it interpolates between corners. A freeze mask then picks which whole blocks mutation may touch. Wires, connections, lookup-table count, and flip-flop count never move, because the genome is nothing but I N I T floats. No operator exists that could move them. That matters, because a phrase like genetic hardware implies topology search. This is narrower: evolutionary search over truth-table parameters on a fixed graph. Useful for inverse design or targeted repair. Not structural logic synthesis.
scenes.headline: Topology stays fixed; INIT values move
scenes.subhead: 64 Float32 entries per LUT6 · frozen or mutable by block

scenes.voiceover: The strongest controlled example is deliberately tiny. A two-bit adder built from four lookup tables, scheduled in two execution levels, meaning two rounds of evaluation where everything inside a round can be computed at once. Four primary input bits, three output bits, so the entire combinational domain is sixteen assignments. The first level computes the low sum with X O R and the low carry with A N D. The second level combines the two upper input bits with that carry. Because every possible input fits on one page, comparing all sixteen rows later is exhaustive for this function rather than a sample. Small does not mean weak evidence here. It means the word proof can be used literally.
scenes.headline: A four-LUT two-bit adder
scenes.subhead: 4 inputs · 3 outputs · 16 complete rows · 2 logic levels
scenes.kicker: The microscope · small enough to exhaust

scenes.voiceover: The targeted experiment freezes the two low-bit tables and lets only the two carry-stage tables move. Sixty-four entries each, so the mutable region is one hundred twenty-eight floats, and every one of them is wiped to zero point five: maximally undecided under this representation. The frozen blocks keep their original binary tables byte for byte, and that is the first falsifiable gate. If mutation or crossover disturbs a single frozen entry, the test fails. It is worth being precise about what is being asked here. The carry-stage tables were declared as all zeros to begin with, so there is no correct answer hiding underneath the wipe. The search has to discover the carry logic, not remember it, while the rest of the circuit stays fixed.
scenes.headline: Two LUTs frozen, two LUTs melted
scenes.subhead: 128 mutable floats wiped to 0.5 · 128 frozen floats preserved
scenes.kicker: Freeze what is known · erase what is not

scenes.voiceover: The implemented search is evolutionary, not gradient descent. Forty-eight chromosomes, each one a full copy of the lookup-table entries. Sparse Gaussian mutation nudges mutable values, occasional jumps land exactly on zero or one, and crossover swaps whole sixty-four-entry blocks between parents. The objective has two terms. The first is what the code calls crypto fitness: the negative sum of squared output error, so zero is perfect and everything else is worse. The second is a binarity penalty, the sum of w times one minus w over every mutable entry, which is zero at zero and at one and largest at one half. Its lambda weight sits at nothing for the first tenth of the run and then ramps up, so the search fits the target first and feels pressure toward binary tables later. The two-bit control pins all of it: one hundred twenty generations, seed hexadecimal seven A six E one seven, a lambda ceiling of twelve, and one binary polish attempt at the end.
scenes.headline: Mutation, crossover, target error, binarity pressure
scenes.subhead: Population 48 · 120 generations · fixed seed 0x7A6E17

scenes.voiceover: Polish proposes a discrete chromosome by thresholding each mutable entry at zero point five. Below becomes zero, at or above becomes one. HELUT then re-scores that hard version against the same target and accepts it only if hard crypto fitness comes out no more than zero point zero zero one worse than the soft version it would replace. That is a real safety gate, and it deserves an accurate name. It is a check against this experiment's target, not a theorem about equivalence. Zero fractional entries tells you the result is discrete. On its own it tells you nothing about whether the result is right.
scenes.headline: Snap at 0.5, then score again
scenes.subhead: Accept only if hard target fitness stays within 0.001
scenes.kicker: Thresholding is a proposal, not a proof

scenes.voiceover: I reran the release test suite this morning. The targeted two-bit melt passed in one point zero nine two seconds, inside a six-test freeze-mask suite that reported zero failures. Its assertions are specific: the frozen tables must stay byte-identical, the mutable region must come back with nothing left in the fractional band between zero point zero five and zero point nine five, and final fitness must beat negative zero point zero five. That proves the harness can discover an acceptable discrete solution for this target and this seed while honoring its freeze mask. It does not prove the searched result survives contact with hardware. Nothing in that test emits Verilog, calls Yosys, or re-checks the sixteen rows afterward.
scenes.label: ARCHIVED RECEIPT PLAYBACK · preserved 2026-09-05 log · not a fresh test run

scenes.voiceover: A different test closes the hardware loop. It takes the unmutated four-table adder, emits it as six-input L U T Verilog, hands the file to Yosys, maps it with A B C, the logic mapper Yosys calls, writes a fresh JSON netlist, reloads that netlist, and compares three outputs across all sixteen inputs. Forty-eight output bits, all agreeing. Then the negative control flips one I N I T entry and runs the same loop. Today's run reported four mismatches, which are exactly the four input patterns that address the corrupted entry. Worth noting that the assertion only demands at least one mismatch, so four is observed behavior rather than a pinned contract. Either way the gate has teeth. But these remain two separate receipts. Targeted search on one side, identity emission on the other.
scenes.headline: Emit → Yosys → reload → exhaust all rows
scenes.subhead: 48 output bits agree · corrupted INIT observed: 4 mismatches

scenes.voiceover: The archived M four run is the counterweight, and it used a different configuration from the two-bit control: population sixteen, lambda ceiling ten, a hundred fifty generations of exploring followed by two hundred fifty of squeezing. Exploring means chasing target fitness with the binarity penalty switched off. Squeezing means turning that penalty up to force the entries binary. The graph held nine hundred twenty-five lookup tables and forty-nine flip-flops, sixteen tables mutable and nine hundred nine frozen. Exploring worked: sampled fitness climbed from minus four point two five to minus one point nine. Squeezing did not. It finished with one hundred eighteen entries still non-binary and target fitness back down at minus four point nine four. A Verilog file came out anyway, because the emitter thresholds whatever it is handed. No equivalence check ever said that file was correct, so this is a failure, not a near-success parked behind an artifact path. The project's answer was to stop searching for plugboard reciprocity in truth-table entries and enforce it structurally instead.
scenes.headline: A larger targeted melt did not freeze
scenes.subhead: 925 LUT · 49 DFF · 16 mutable · 118 entries still fractional
scenes.kicker: The failure stays in the ledger

scenes.voiceover: So how does this compare with logic simplification as it already exists? Yosys and A B C rewrite Boolean structure. They remove redundancy, merge cells, map to a target library, and trade depth against area. The HELUT search holds structure still and changes lookup-table values to fit a target while pushing them toward binary. Its objective carries no area term, no depth term, no power or timing term. And the emitter writes exactly one L U T six per original lookup table, so emission alone can never reduce the count. A combined flow is easy to describe: discover a new discrete function on fixed topology, emit it, then let A B C strip whatever redundancy that creates. Until that flow runs end to end and reports fewer tables or lower depth under identical mapping, HELUT has not demonstrated better simplification. It has demonstrated a different knob.
scenes.headline: HELUT and ABC optimize different things
scenes.subhead: Fixed truth tables versus structural rewriting and mapping

scenes.voiceover: Four rows, then. One: a Yosys lookup-table graph can be lifted into continuous truth-table parameters and evaluated on Metal. Two: a freeze mask protects known tables while a deterministic evolutionary search discovers an acceptable discrete solution in the two-bit control. Three: unmutated TensorLUT Verilog survives Yosys re-synthesis and exhaustive checking, and the checker catches a one-bit corruption. Four: those two lanes are not joined. Searched elites do get emitted in other tests, but nothing re-synthesizes one and re-proves it, and there is no area or depth win over A B C to point at. That join is a precise engineering task now rather than an open question. Melt and freeze is real. General logic simplification is still a hypothesis with named gates in front of it.
scenes.headline: What melt/freeze proves today
scenes.subhead: Representation: yes. Controlled rediscovery: yes. General simplification: open.
